title_guess: Basel accords, part 1: why banks fail, the three bank risks, BIS and the Basel Committee (capital adequacy terms only introduced)
recurring_cast: 'type of risks' stem with three red risk names (credit, market, operational), later docked as a left sidebar
running_examples: story, not numbers: public deposits and market money flow into a bank, the bank lends to a person, the person does not repay, the bank fails (credit risk)
facts: BIS set up 1930 in Basel, owned by 62 central banks (~95% of world GDP); BCBS 1974, G10; Basel I 1988, II 2004, III 2010

best_moments.why: credit risk as a story: deposit and market arrows feed the bank, the loan goes out, the interest return loop is crossed with a red X, a FAIL seal stamps the bank, and a long dotted curve files the event under 'credit risk' in the sidebar
a red FAIL seal stamps onto the bank icon at the start: the stakes of the whole topic in one object
BIS as a hub: two-headed arrows to five central banks around it make 'a club where central banks meet' visible
the Basel Committee drawn as a long committee table with a row of heads: 'a committee' becomes a picture, not a word
summary: a yellow RBI column drops between the Basel accords (right) and the bank with its risks (left); dotted arrows carry the rules through RBI to the bank: who makes the rule vs who applies it

weak_moments.why: consequences of bank failure are four text bullets; contagion and credit crunch are never drawn
CAR, CRAR and RWA appear only as abbreviation lines; the ratio the title promises is never shown as a ratio (no capital vs risky-assets picture)
market risk is a list of four asset names plus a note that prices swing; no price line moves
operational risk is a four-word list under a bank icon
BIS facts (oldest, 1930, Basel) as plain text lines

segments.teaches: a bank faces credit, market and operational risk; if it fails, depositors lose savings, trust falls, failure spreads to other banks, credit dries up and the economy slows

segments.notes: 7 change events (~every 10 s). The FAIL seal is a strong single picture; the consequence chain that follows is just a list.
segments.idea: risks can make a bank fail, and one failure hurts savers, trust, other banks and lending, ending in a downturn
segments.shown_as: a bank icon drops a stem to a 'type of risks' label with three red risk names beneath; a red FAIL seal stamps onto the bank; to the right four consequence bullets write on one by one, capped by a framed 'economic downturn' banner

segments.teaches: the BIS Basel accords (I, II, III) answer bank risk by asking banks to hold capital; how much is judged by CAR / CRAR on risk-weighted assets; capital is split into tier I and tier II

elements.what: dark grey panel slides over the risk tree as a frame
BIS emblem with its full name, sitting on the panel's top edge
Basel accords tag with Basel I / II / III chips on the panel edge
line from a wavy brace on the three risks to a 'capital' tag
capital splits into tier I and tier II
'how to decide?' then three abbreviation lines (CAR, CRAR, RWA) with arrows to full names

segments.notes: 9 change events (~every 7 s). The capital idea never becomes a picture (no cushion or buffer under the bank) and the ratio is never drawn; this video stops before the actual CAR rules.
segments.idea: the global answer to bank risk is to make banks keep their own capital as a cushion, measured against their risky assets
segments.shown_as: a dark grey panel slides over the risk list, framed by the BIS mark and Basel I/II/III chips; a brace on the three risks draws a line to a 'capital' tag, which splits into tier I and tier II; under it 'how to decide?' leads to three ratio abbreviations

segments.teaches: BIS is a hub where central banks exchange information, cooperate and promote stability; it gives banking services only to central banks and international bodies

segments.teaches: BIS hosts the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (1974; G10 central bank governors), which developed the Basel norms, now called the Basel accords, for a sound and stable global banking system

segments.teaches: a bank earns its income as interest on loans; more lending means more income but also more risk

segments.idea: lending earns interest, and the more a bank lends the more it earns but the more it can lose

segments.teaches: the money a bank lends comes from public deposits and from the market (equity, debt); if a borrower does not repay, the bank cannot repay them and fails: credit risk

elements.what: dense crowd labelled public with a 'deposit' arrow into the bank
two 'market' labels sending 'equity' and 'debt' arrows into the bank
red X on the dotted interest-return loop
red FAIL seal stamped on the bank
box around 'credit risk' in the sidebar
long dotted curve from the loan's RISK label down and back to the sidebar's credit-risk entry

segments.notes: 8 change events (~every 6 s). Best segment: default is shown as a broken return loop and a stamp, and then filed under its name.
segments.idea: a bank lends other people's money, so a borrower who does not repay can sink the bank: that is credit risk
segments.shown_as: a public crowd sends a deposit arrow into the bank and two market labels send equity and debt arrows; the bank lends on to a person; then the return loop above is crossed with a red X, a red FAIL seal stamps the bank, and a long dotted curve swoops from the loan's RISK label to the boxed 'credit risk' entry in the sidebar

segments.teaches: a bank also invests in gold, securities and bonds, shares and real estate; their prices move, so it can lose money: market risk

segments.shown_as: the sidebar boxes 'market risk'; the bank sends an 'invests' arrow to a four-item list (gold, bonds, shares, property) and a red-ruled note says some of these swing in price
